Web Teardown
Product analysis · reconstruction-grade UX/UI specification

Claude of Tanks

A feature-rich browser armored-combat simulator that pairs a massive vehicle library with unusually explicit ballistic, armor, module and crew feedback. Its differentiator is not merely “tanks in a browser”; it is a learning surface that lets the player see why a shot worked.

01 · Executive verdict

A simulation playground with a competitive-game shell

Claude of Tanks wins on inspectability: garage dossiers, diagnostic gallery layers, live hit reasons and a post-death X-ray turn hidden combat math into readable cause and effect. The product is already broad enough to feel like a platform; its main design problem is teaching players which part of that platform matters first.

9/10System transparency
8/10Content breadth
6/10First-session focus
8/10Reconstruction complexity
Product thesis. Position the game as an explorable armored-combat laboratory that happens to support full battles. The battlefield supplies tension; the garage, gallery, analysis panels and replay supply understanding and long-term mastery.
02 · Why the concept works

Scale attracts; explanation differentiates

Instant fantasy

Modern armored vehicles, national fleets and large outdoor battlefields create a legible fantasy before the player learns any rules.

Mechanical credibility

Shell types, impact angle, effective armor, internal modules, crew, repairs and directional damage establish a coherent simulation vocabulary.

Inspectable depth

Gallery diagnostics, technical manuals and kill analysis convert invisible systems into objects the player can study and compare.

The distinctive product stack

BrowseChoose a country, class, generation and vehicle.
InspectRead armor, modules, crew and ammunition.
DeploySelect a battlefield and battle context.
FightMove, aim, select shells and manage damage.
UnderstandReview penetration and destruction evidence.
Core competitive advantage: most combat games summarize outcomes as damage numbers. Here, the UI can teach armor geometry, ammunition choice and subsystem risk without leaving the match.
03 · Product definition

Three products sharing one simulation

LayerUser jobPrimary surfacesValue

Likely primary audience

Desktop players who already understand tank-game conventions and want a zero-install technical sandbox with broad vehicle access.

Secondary audience

Vehicle enthusiasts, developers and technically curious players who enjoy comparing models, armor layouts and simulation behaviors.

04 · Observed session

From catalog curiosity to a complete combat learning cycle

  1. The session opens in the garage on an M1A3 Abrams, then inspects national fleets, vehicle statistics, armor, modules, crew and ammunition.
  2. The battle menu exposes bot play, private rooms, local-network play and five solo rules.
  3. Settings reveal a full keyboard/mouse command map, aim behavior, audio groups, visual presets, language and difficulty.
  4. Scene Studio demonstrates free-camera vehicle staging, state controls, layers and scripted effects.
  5. Tank Gallery presents a searchable archive, operational profile, view presets, articulation controls and diagnostic overlays.
  6. Documentation explains the simulation architecture, content scale and networking model.
  7. A seven-versus-seven bot battle proceeds from loading roster through movement, targeting, penetration, module damage, repairs, a kill, destruction, kill analysis and allied spectating.
  8. The player returns to the garage, closing the loop where another vehicle or battlefield can be selected.
7v7Observed battle size
3Shell slots on selected tank
3Damage-control consumables
1Fully observed battle
05 · Core loop

Select → learn → deploy → diagnose → adapt

1 · SelectVehicle, nation, battlefield and battle type.
2 · PrepareRead armor, ammunition, systems and controls.
3 · ManeuverUse terrain, team positions, sight lines and minimap.
4 · EngageAim, choose a shell, lead the target and fire.
5 · ReadPenetration, block, ricochet, damage and module outcome.
6 · RecoverReposition, repair, treat crew or extinguish fire.
7 · ContinueSpectate or return to the fleet and change the setup.

Decision cadence

CadenceDecisionInformation needed
Pre-battleWhich vehicle and map context?Nation, class, era, protection, firepower, mobility and special system.
TraversalWhere to move and expose armor?Minimap, team state, terrain, detection and directional threat.
EngagementWhich target, surface and shell?Range, reload, target silhouette, armor feedback and remaining ammunition.
After impactRepeat, change aim, change shell or disengage?Outcome label, effective armor, angle, penetration reserve and affected systems.
After damageSpend a consumable now or preserve it?HP, track/module status, crew status, fire state and cooldown.
06 · Controls & interaction model

A dense desktop command set with strong categorization

DomainDefault interactionReconstruction behavior
HullW/S throttle, A/D steer, Space handbrake, F flip recovery.Continuous input; braking and pivot intent must remain independent of turret aim.
WeaponLeft click fire, Shift sniper, number keys choose shells, E special system, C magazine reload.Fire is gated by reload and ammunition; selected shell state must update instantly even when reload continues.
Damage control4 repair, 5 first aid, 6 extinguisher.Each action validates its target condition and returns explicit “used”, “unneeded” or cooldown feedback.
Camera / aimRight button aim or free-look mode, wheel zoom, optional hold/toggle behavior.Input mode must be user-selectable; pointer lock and camera restoration require clear escape behavior.
Tactical UIM minimap zoom, L shot log, Escape settings.Overlays must not consume steering/fire input after close; focus state is restored to the canvas.
Onboarding risk: the command list is comprehensive, but battle entry does not visibly stage it. A first-run overlay should teach only drive, aim, fire, shell switching and repair; advanced bindings can remain in settings.
07 · Rules & combat model

Reconstruction model

Hit resolution pipeline

Ray / projectileResolve world-space path and struck surface.
AngleCompute impact normal and effective plate thickness.
ShellApply penetration model, distance loss and ammunition behavior.
OutcomePenetration, block, ricochet or non-damaging contact.
InternalsTrace through modules, crew and damage zones.
FeedbackShow HP, critical/module state and readable reason.

Observed battle rules

  • Two teams begin with seven vehicles, with living roster counts and team score in the top band.
  • Vehicles have hit points plus a more granular internal state represented by tank schematic, modules and crew.
  • Incoming hits may be blocked, ricochet, deal ordinary damage, or produce critical/module effects.
  • Track destruction immobilizes the vehicle until repaired; dedicated repair, crew and fire consumables handle different failure classes.
  • Shell inventory is finite by type. When a type is depleted, the next available ammunition can be selected automatically.
  • Detection is explicit: the player receives a visible notice when an opponent gains visual contact.
  • After destruction, a replay explains the fatal shot, then the player may spectate living allies or return to the garage.
08 · Progression & difficulty

Horizontal mastery is visible; account progression is not

Content progression

Nation tabs, era labels, vehicle classes, maps and rule variants offer a broad matrix of scenarios without requiring a traditional linear campaign.

Skill progression

Players learn armor presentation, shell choice, weak zones, range, reload timing, terrain use and damage-control prioritization.

Difficulty controls

Bot difficulty is explicitly selectable. The observed route used the normal setting, while other levels were available but not exercised.

What was not established

  • No account level, currency, unlock cost, research tree or monetization loop was observed.
  • No ranked result, rating movement, achievement, daily task or long-term profile summary was exercised.
  • The large fleet appears primarily as accessible content in the observed build; whether every vehicle is immediately usable in every context is not confirmed.
Design implication: retention should lean first on mastery, comparison and scenario discovery. Adding a heavy grind would conflict with the browser build’s strongest promise: immediate access to the simulation.

10 · Feedback hierarchy

Four channels explain every consequential shot

ChannelPlacementPurposePriority
World feedbackAt target or player vehicleMuzzle flash, impact, debris, explosion, nameplate, HP delta.Immediate perception.
Directional feedbackAround central aim areaSource direction plus block, ricochet, damage or critical classification.Immediate response.
Shot historyLeft-side event stackPersistent recent record of source, shell, zone and affected systems.Short-term diagnosis.
Ballistic analysisRight-side panel or death replayShell, target, range, angle, nominal/effective armor, penetration and diagrams.Learning and mastery.

Semantic language

Green

Allies, team-positive state and friendly labels.

Red

Enemies, damage, disabled systems and lethal threat.

Amber

Selected action, ammunition, analysis emphasis and system warning.

White / gray

Neutral telemetry, inactive controls, labels and reference values.

Information-density rule: never show more than one expanded analysis panel per shot. New results replace the previous panel while the compact event stack preserves history; otherwise battle feedback becomes a wall of competing diagnostics.
11 · Return loop & retention

The fleet is the backlog; mastery is the reward

Short-term

After death, spectator and garage actions keep the next decision close. A different vehicle, battlefield or rule can be selected without leaving the application.

Mid-term

National fleets, vehicle generations, map rotation and bot difficulty create a natural checklist of matchups to learn.

Long-term

Private and local rooms could convert individual experimentation into social sessions; deeper armor and module knowledge compounds across vehicles.

Retention gaps

  • No observed “recent vehicles”, favorites, saved loadouts or compare queue reduces the cost of navigating a very large catalog.
  • No battle result summary was reached, so rewards, match history and post-match learning prompts remain unknown.
  • The garage exposes many dimensions at once but does not visibly recommend a next learning goal.
  • Social-room persistence is documented, but invite, reconnect and host-migration behavior was not exercised.
Best retention extension: a “Mastery Lab” card that proposes one vehicle/map/ammunition lesson per visit and saves the matching Gallery diagnostic preset. It creates goals from systems already present instead of inventing a separate reward economy.

13 · Acquisition & growth

A compelling technical pitch, not validated audience momentum

26Creator-post score at snapshot
0Verified independent actors
100+Vehicle-scale acquisition hook
WatchEvidence posture

The public counter is engagement on a creator-authored development post, not a player, launch, retention or revenue metric. No independent spread was verified in the dated discovery snapshot.

Acquisition model

The likely hook is a three-part demonstration: a huge playable fleet in a browser, deep armor and module simulation, and destruction explained by an X-ray replay. The first promise earns the click; the second and third distinguish the product after arrival.

Strong share assets

  • Rapid fleet montage across nations and eras.
  • One shot transitioning from impact to ballistic panel to X-ray.
  • Scene Studio staging a recognizable vehicle matchup.
  • Direct browser link that opens on a recommended starter vehicle.

Growth risks

  • The build’s scope may be discussed more than its moment-to-moment play.
  • The AI-assisted production story can overshadow product quality.
  • Genre comparisons raise expectations for polish, matchmaking and progression.
  • Large content numbers invite scrutiny of vehicle fidelity and balance.

Recommended landing sequence

  1. Lead with “Choose a tank and play now” rather than architecture or production story.
  2. Offer three curated starters: forgiving heavy armor, mobile scout, precision gun platform.
  3. After the first successful penetration, expose the full analysis and link to Gallery.
  4. After the first battle, invite the player to copy a private-room code or share the exact matchup.

Public sources: playable browser build · creator development post · public repository.

14 · Development model

Agent-assisted production with explicit ownership and visual proof loops

The project is publicly presented as a solo-directed build in which Kevin B. Liu set product direction while Claude Code agents handled bounded subsystem work and Codex supported parallel development and review. The important story is not automation alone; it is the control structure around it.

Confirmed stack

  • Three.js for browser rendering and 3D presentation.
  • Vite for the development/build shell.
  • WebSocket networking for room connectivity, prediction and authoritative state paths.
  • Claude Code for multi-agent subsystem implementation.
  • Codex for parallel development and review work.

Process controls

  • Persistent agent instructions establish units, deterministic behavior and release gates.
  • Vehicle families can be assigned to separate owners rather than edited concurrently.
  • Isolated worktrees reduce conflicts across parallel tasks.
  • Visual critics inspect screenshots for proportion, clipping, surfaces and running gear.
  • Changes pass a loop of render, inspect, measure and rerun.

What the iteration history suggests

An early one-shot prototype did not provide enough quality. Subsequent work expanded vehicle and map fidelity, missiles, abilities, destruction, the Gallery and Scene Studio while adding stricter verification. This is a useful production lesson: for a spatial simulation, textual checks are necessary but insufficient; camera framing, proportions, articulation and overlap need direct visual review.

Reconstruction takeaway: treat each vehicle as a data-and-validation package, not merely a model. Geometry, armor zones, internal modules, crew, articulation, ammunition, balance, camera bounds and network serialization must ship together.

Primary references: repository and project documentation · creator-authored production overview.

7. Gallery and Studio contracts

  • Gallery search must tokenize display name, family, nation, class and era; results update without camera reset.
  • View presets interpolate camera over 250–400 ms and preserve zoom within safe bounds.
  • Diagnostic layers are mutually composable only when the resulting visual remains readable; otherwise use radio behavior with a clear active label.
  • Articulation sliders write to reversible pose state and expose reset-all.
  • Studio scene state is serializable: battlefield, tank, transform, paint, damage state, layer visibility, event list and effect triggers.
17 · Acceptance criteria

Definition of reconstruction-complete

Functional

  • Vehicle selection updates model, dossier, ammunition, armor, modules and crew from one definition.
  • Bots populate two teams, navigate a battlefield, acquire targets and resolve shots through the same authoritative hit pipeline as the player.
  • Hull, turret and gun inputs operate independently; chase, free-look and scoped cameras restore state correctly.
  • All shell inventories, reload states and auto-selection transitions remain internally consistent.
  • Penetration uses impact angle and zone thickness; the displayed analysis exactly matches the resolved result.
  • Module, crew, track and fire states modify the vehicle and map to the correct consumable.
  • Detection, roster, score, minimap and spectator states update from the same battle entity lifecycle.
  • Fatal-shot data survives into replay and X-ray without recomputation drift.
  • Garage, Gallery and Studio share the same vehicle assets and articulation definitions.
  • Private-room codes and local-network discovery recover from invalid, full and disconnected states.

UX / visual

  • Primary HUD remains collision-free at 1280×720, 1920×1080 and ultrawide aspect ratios.
  • All combat-critical text meets 4.5:1 contrast and supports a 125% interface scale.
  • Ally/enemy/outcome semantics remain distinguishable without color through position, icon and label.
  • Every binding is remappable; conflicts are identified before save.
  • Reticle, hit result and repair prompts remain readable over bright sky, terrain and explosions.
  • Expanded analysis can be dismissed without blocking movement or fire.
  • Gallery filters and vehicle carousel are fully keyboard navigable.
  • Settings preserve input, sound, visual and language choices across reload.
  • Reduced-motion mode limits camera sweeps, screen shake and repeated warning pulses.
  • Kill analysis labels never overlap the projectile path or selected internal component.

Critical test scenarios

  1. Fire three shell types at the same plate from two angles and verify distinct but reproducible outcomes and explanations.
  2. Destroy a track, activate the wrong consumable, then the correct one; confirm validation messages and state restoration.
  3. Deplete the selected shell type during reload; verify the next valid shell selection and HUD synchronization.
  4. Destroy a vehicle with a projectile crossing multiple internal systems; confirm the live result and replay path are identical.
  5. Die while team members remain; cycle every living ally, then return to Garage without stale battle input.
  6. Switch vehicle in Gallery, toggle armor/modules/crew, return to Garage and verify no diagnostic material leaks into the normal model.

19 · Evidence & confidence

What can be trusted

Claim areaConfidenceBasis
Garage, settings, Studio, Gallery, Docs, bot battle, death replay and spectator flowHighDirectly observed across the complete recorded session and saved images.
Combat HUD, shell switching, detection, block/ricochet, penetration, module damage and consumablesHighDirectly exercised or explicitly surfaced by the running product.
Fleet and battlefield totals, fixed-step simulation, local bots and room/authority architectureHighExplicit in the in-product documentation and consistent with public project materials.
Private-room, local-network and dedicated ranked behaviorMediumEntry points and architectural claims exist, but those paths were not exercised.
Later match resolution, result/reward flow and multi-battle progressionUnknownThe observed battle ended in player destruction and exited through spectator/garage.
Audience, active population, retention, revenue and durable growthUnknownThe public snapshot provides a creator post and repository, not product analytics.

Unobserved surfaces that need a second pass

  • Host/join errors, room reconnect, local-network discovery and dedicated competitive flow.
  • A complete team victory or defeat and its result, reward, rematch and history states.
  • Creation/editing in the camouflage surface and persistence of saved loadouts.
  • Multiple vehicles in battle, especially missile, magazine and unusual-ability archetypes.
  • Touch controls, narrow layouts, gamepad edge cases and installation lifecycle.

Scope note: this teardown is based on the latest complete recorded play package, its saved images, product text and a dated Browser Game Radar snapshot. Public metrics may have changed since the snapshot. Recommendations and implementation models are reconstruction choices where the product does not disclose an exact rule.
